notes.meaning: Ziklag was a Philistine town. Achish, king of Gath, gave it to David as a safe place to hide from Saul. David was still held back there, not yet able to take up the role God had chosen him for. Even while David stayed hidden, God was quietly moving brave men to come and stand with him.

These fighters were from Benjamin, Saul's own tribe. They were skilled archers and slingers who could use either hand, a prized gift in battle (see Judges 20:16). They had much to gain if Saul stayed king. Yet they chose David, because they saw that God had left Saul and was with David.

Here the leaders of the Benjamite band are named, starting with their chief, Ahiezer. Some came from towns like Gibeah and Anathoth, a town for priests. Ishmaiah belonged to "the Thirty," David's special group of heroes, and at times led them. His name may be missing from the list in chapter 11 because he had died by then.

The list goes on. The Korahites were from the tribe of Levi. Their families had guarded the entrance to God's tent. They lived among the Benjamites, and their service at God's house may have stirred them to fight for David, God's chosen man. Some of these families also lived in towns of Judah, like Gedor.

Some men of Gad, from east of the Jordan, broke away from their fellow Gadites who stayed loyal to Saul. They came to David's hideout in the wilderness. Many of David's earlier followers were people in trouble or debt, but these were trained soldiers. They were skilled with shield and spear, fierce as lions, and swift as gazelles, which was highly valued in ancient war.
The Gadite leaders are listed one by one in order of rank: first, second, third, and so on. Their names are kept as a lasting honor for their readiness to help the man God had chosen to rule.
The list ends with the eleventh man. They were only eleven, but they added much to David's strength.

These Gadites were top warriors. The weakest of them could take on a hundred men, and the strongest a thousand. This is a strong figure of speech to show how brave they were (compare Leviticus 26:8). Some older readers took it to mean they were officers over hundreds and thousands back in their own tribe.

The first month is the spring month of Nisan, about March to April. Then melting snow made the Jordan flood its banks, and crossing was very dangerous. These men crossed anyway, probably fighting their way through Saul's supporters on both sides of the river. Nothing would keep them from their king when he needed them.

More men from Benjamin and Judah came to David's hideout. The Benjamites may have brought men of Judah along so David would not suspect them. Their names are not given, except for their leader, Amasai.

David had been betrayed before by men of Judah, so he met these men with care. He made a fair offer: if they came in peace, his heart would be joined to theirs. If they came to betray him, he would not take revenge himself. He left it to "the God of our fathers," the God they all shared, to see and judge.

The Spirit of God came on Amasai. Literally, the Spirit "clothed" him. He was given courage and the right words, not a prophecy. He pledged complete loyalty to David, called him "son of Jesse" as a mark of honor, and blessed him with peace because they could see God was helping him. David welcomed them and made them leaders. In the same way, believers should belong to Jesus wholly and stand openly on His side.

Some men from Manasseh joined David when he marched with the Philistines toward the battle against Saul (see 1 Samuel 29). The Philistine rulers sent David away. They feared he would turn on them in battle and win back Saul's favor at the cost of their heads. These men came to help David, not the Philistines.

As David headed back to Ziklag, seven leaders from Manasseh joined him. This was before the battle in which Saul died. They were "chiefs of thousands," heads of the large family groups who led Manasseh's fighting men.

The "raiders" were the Amalekites, who had burned Ziklag and carried off the women and children while David was away (1 Samuel 30). These brave Manasseh leaders helped David chase them down. Help arrived just when David needed it.

Day after day more men came, until David had a great army. "Like the army of God" means very great and mighty, a host in which God's power could be seen. Its greatness lay in its strength and spirit, not only in numbers. A band that began with distressed men became a remarkable army under God and David.

This next list comes years later, after the death of Saul's son Ish-bosheth. The tribes came to Hebron to make David king over all Israel, as God had promised. They came armed in case anyone opposed them. The list starts with the southern tribes, then the northern ones, and ends with those east of the Jordan.

Judah and Simeon sent fairly small numbers. David had already been king over Judah for about seven years, and Simeon lived inside Judah's land. So they sent men on behalf of their whole tribe. Living nearby, they also had to host and feed those who came from far away.

Even Levites and priests came, ready to fight for David as well as pray for him, because they knew God had called him. Jehoiada was not the high priest (that was Abiathar). He was the leader of the fighting men from Aaron's family. Zadok, a brave young man, came with 22 officers from his family. The Law never forbade Levites from serving as soldiers.
Only 3,000 came from Benjamin, Saul's tribe. Up to then, most of them had tried to keep the crown in Saul's family. Loyalty to family should never overrule a good conscience.

Ephraim sent famous warriors, though fewer than might be expected. Their tribe may have been weakened by recent wars. From the half of Manasseh west of the Jordan came 18,000, chosen by name. They were not ashamed to openly declare David their king.

The men of Issachar were wise. They understood the times: public affairs, the mood of the nation, and where events were heading. They backed Saul while he lived, then knew this was the moment Israel should make David king. Their people trusted their lead. If we lack such wisdom, we can ask God, who gives freely.

Zebulun sent 50,000 well-trained soldiers who could keep in formation. The Hebrew says they were "without a heart and a heart." That means they were not two-faced: they did not pretend to back David while secretly favoring Saul's family. They had warm hearts but cool heads.
Naphtali, Dan, and Asher, tribes of the north, sent large numbers. These tribes had been less harmed by earlier wars, so they could send many men. These are estimates by army units, not a head count.
The tribes east of the Jordan sent the most of all, 120,000. Those who lived farthest away showed their eagerness by bringing so many. Wisely, they also brought their own weapons.

All these soldiers came to Hebron with one firm purpose: to make David king over all Israel. The rest of the nation agreed. No one was out for himself; all sought the good of the whole people. David did not force his rule on them; he waited until they were willing.
They feasted with David for three days. Their fellow Israelites who lived nearby had prepared the food. Probably not every soldier sat at the feast, but mainly the leaders sent by each tribe.

People came from near and far, as far north as Issachar, Zebulun, and Naphtali, with loads of food on animals. All wanted the celebration to be generous and fitting. There was joy in Israel, because a good king was taking the throne. In the same way, when Christ is made King in a heart, there is great joy that lasts not three days but forever.
